items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
items.content:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.

The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."

Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.

Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.

Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

items.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
items.summary: browsers
items.content:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

items.title: Pro-Palestinian websites targeted in cyberattack on Icelandic hosting company
items.content:
Pro-Palestinian websites targeted in cyberattack on Icelandic hosting company

Mörður Áslaugarson says the hackers' likely objective was to target websites supporting Palestine.

The hackers behind a major cyberattack on Icelandic web hosting company 1984 ehf. yesterday appear to have been aiming to destroy websites supporting Palestine.

This is according to Mörður Áslaugarson, the company's managing director, who says the hackers managed to destroy seven such websites before they were stopped. That is probably the only damage caused by the attack.

The company temporarily shut down all its services yesterday after discovering that a cyberattack was underway.

"We have stopped all activity by these attackers. In fact, we did that quite some time ago, yesterday. But now we need to go through everything they might have done, remove all traces of their activity and thoroughly clean up after them. That's the phase we're in now, the cleanup phase," says Áslaugarson, adding that cybersecurity company Syndis is handling the cleanup.

"At the same time, we're preparing our systems to bring our services back online, one by one."

Asked whether there is any indication of when the company's services can be restored, he says:

"Not yet. We'll be able to answer that today. We don't want to make promises we can't keep. We simply don't think that would be acceptable. So we'll have to accept that people are unhappy about our inability to provide a timeline. But we want to be certain that whatever we say will prove broadly accurate."

Can he give any indication of the timeframe? Is it a matter of days?

"It varies somewhat depending on the service. Email and DNS services should be back up this weekend, preferably today or overnight into tomorrow. We're working around the clock," says Áslaugarson.

"Then we'll try to restore customers' virtual servers. We provide a service called VPS, or Virtual Private Server, and we hope to have that service running again by late tomorrow or Monday. It all depends on when we're confident that security has been fully restored. That's our primary concern."

"It's a bit like having an uninvited guest enter your home. They weren't particularly tidy and left dirt here and there. We want to make sure there's no dirt left anywhere before we let others back in to use the premises," he adds.

As previously mentioned, the hackers' original objective appears to have been to destroy websites expressing support for the Palestinian people. After damaging seven such websites, they attempted to spread further through 1984's systems.

Asked whether any additional damage has been identified beyond the destruction of the websites, Áslaugarson says he believes it is unlikely to have been extensive.

"We caught them almost immediately. We spotted them very quickly and disrupted their activities right from the start, so they never had the opportunity to do much more. Eventually, we shut everything down so we could work undisturbed rather than having to keep fighting them," he says.

"So we're not particularly pessimistic. In fact, we're very optimistic that, apart from the damaged websites, the main impact will simply be the inconvenience caused by the service outage."

items.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
items.content:
“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

Surveillance pricing versus dynamic pricing

Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center ( EPIC ), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”

“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains .

Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.

Dynamic pricing , or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.

While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.

For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

ZipRecruiter was one of the first companies to leverage surveillance pricing as we think of it today. In 2018, its profits increased 84 percent by using surveillance pricing versus charging every customer $99. Surveillance pricing is still somewhat nascent, but its potential lucrativeness and the growing availability of user data suggest it may become more common.

Other technological advancements, including advanced machine-learning methods, have further facilitated the growth of personalized pricing.

In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

According to a 2025 statement from then-FTC Chair Lina M. Khan, “retailers frequently use people’s personal information to set targeted, tailored prices for goods and services—from a person’s location and demographics, down to their mouse movements on a webpage.”

Surveillance pricing has become more widespread as food delivery platforms, rideshare services, rental housing providers, and other businesses have gained access to the technology and data needed to implement it. Third-party data brokers, advertising and analytics companies, and credit providers make it easy for organizations to get the information needed to build customer profiles. The growth of web browsing, the Internet of Things, and user tracking have created data-rich digital lives that are simple for retailers to analyze.

items.title: Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
items.summary: mobile, privacy
items.content:
Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is really about the death of the American Dream
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is really about the death of the American Dream

Even when they were well written, every GTA story has ultimately been about solving your problems with the accumulation of wealth. But Grand Theft Auto 6 specifically focuses on the systemic issues that make any version of the American Dream — saving money, buying a home and supporting a family with a fulfilling job — incredibly difficult for people living on the margins of society. The crushing weight of capitalism is always pressing down on you, just like in the real world.

Lucia Caminos committed an ill-conceived robbery, is subsequently sent to jail and is forced to claw her way back into civilian life with little support. Jason Duval joined the Army to escape his troubled youth and ends up serving as muscle for a small-time criminal. Much like the real Bonnie and Clyde, Lucia and Jason are driven by the need to escape poverty, but it's up to you to determine if they'll share a similar end.

I only have around 12 hours of GTA 6 under my belt so far (it's estimated to take around 50 hours to beat, and hundreds of hours to fully complete), but Rockstar clearly frames why our lead characters pursue a life of crime: beyond the generational poverty and lack of upward mobility, Lucia and Jason are also trying to build enough stability to reclaim custody of their infant son.

When she decides to stick up a payday loan store (the existence of which is inherently predatory against low-income people ), she's doing it to feed her kid, afford diapers and survive as a single mother. (Jason isn't aware of him at that point in the story.) It's hard to imagine Lucia making such a desperate decision if she had enough social support. But of course, that's not the American way.

Six months worth of baby formula costs upwards of $2,700 in the US,, whereas it's just $759 in the UK. And while America ranks fifth when it comes to the affordability of diapers changes worldwide, that's still around $1,200 a year — a significant cost for poor families. Complementary video: Install and config from the source

A few days ago we saw how to authorise extra repositories for apt-cache to search when we need unusual applications, or perhaps more recent versions than those in the standard repositories.

Today we’re going one step further - literally going to “go to the source”. This is not something to be done lightly - the whole reason for package managers is to make your life easy - but occasionally it is justified, and it is something you need to be aware of and comfortable with.

The applications we’ve been installing up to this point have come from repositories. The files there are “binaries” - pre-compiled, and often customised by your distro. What might not be clear is that your distro gets these applications from a diverse range of un-coordinated development projects (the “upstream”), and these developers are continuously working on new versions. We’ll go to one of these, download the source, compile and install it.

(Another big part of what package managers like apt do, is to identify and install any required “dependencies”. In the Linux world many open source apps take advantage of existing infrastructure in this way, but it can be a very tricky thing to resolve manually. However, the app we’re installing today from source is relatively unusual in being completly standalone).

Projects normally provide their applications as “source files”, written in the C, C++ or other computer languages. We’re going to pull down such a source file, but it won’t be any use to us until we compile it into an “executable” - a program that our server can execute. So, we’ll need to first install a standard bundle of common compilers and similar tools. On Ubuntu, the package of such tools is called “build-essential”. Install it like this:

items.content:
Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell ·

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance . It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Wiki.alpinelinux.org has been languishing a bit

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Is Getting Worse at the Exact Moment That Nvidia Rehired Him: It's metastasizing.
items.content:
Much like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman before him, Nvidia’s leader Jensen Huang was summarily pushed out of the company he founded — only to be reinstated after days of turbulence.

Less than an hour before the opening bell, Nvidia announced on Monday morning that it was reinstating its disgraced CEO “effective immediately” after 11 days of mounting losses . The move, an effort personally spearheaded by president Donald Trump , had investors elated, restoring well over 30 percent of Nvidia’s market value.

But while a triumphant Wall Street pops bottles, the underlying scandal is metastasizing. At the core is the Trump administration’s efforts to clear the path for deals Nvidia struck with Chinese companies, seemingly in defiance of export bans and growing concerns over national security amid the AI race.

As the New York Times reported over the weekend , the woman with whom Huang had an extramarital affair with, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from early 2025 until the fall of this year. Even her husband, Kang Wei, had personally worked with the spy agency, according to the newspaper’s sources.

Put simply, Nvidia’s CEO was having an affair with a woman who seems to have been actively relaying information to China’s intelligence community. While we don’t know what kind of data she managed to gather, it’s the best indication yet that Nvidia’s founder is a possibly compromised target of the Chinese government, further highlighting the stakes at play.

Alice Huang was also an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which has been linked to efforts to smuggle Nvidia’s sought after AI chips into China, evading export control laws.

In other words, Trump appears to be directly aiding the Chinese spy agency’s efforts by ensuring Huang’s reinstatement as the linchpin of not just the AI industry, but increasingly the entire US economy .

According to the NYT , the Trump administration was monitoring Alice Huang’s contact with the spy agency for over a year. Experts told the newspaper that China’s Ministry of State Security is explicitly working to get around US export bans.

In the meantime, Trump took to his social media network, Truth Social, this week to trivialize Huang’s extramarital affairs and play them off as a big joke.

That’s despite knowing full well of what was going on. According to the NYT , Trump was briefed on at least two occasions of Alice Huang’s ties to the Chinese spy agency and her affair.

The president has since denied he knew “that she is a spy.”

“Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said in a Friday statement, while calling for Huang’s reinstatement.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to probe the matter, with senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) calling the decision to bring Huang back as CEO “ reckless .”

So far, scheduled intelligence briefings have either been delayed or raised more questions than answers for lawmakers, as the NYT reports.

Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour .

In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.

In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car.

These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands.

“There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW.

The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app.

The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim-survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf.

It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment.

“Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said.

The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands.

One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people.

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it

difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow

definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116 , which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly

Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside

of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection.

Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:

YAML is a big and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was

invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now

opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec

conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary,

but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet .

Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0 , which was released in 2018 .

However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing)

wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that

version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch ( YamlDotNet#467 ) only fixed the double-quoted

form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: I made usb-rea: point it at a USB capture of a Windows-only vendor app and it writes a Linux driver
items.content:
If you find this useful, you can support me by getting a SkinToScan pack, my other project. It's a one-time purchase that directly funds my open-source work.

usb-rea reads a USB capture (pcap or pcapng, from usbmon or USBPcap) and does the step after Wireshark: it infers the command and protocol structure from labelled actions, then writes a Markdown report and a standalone pyusb driver. I built it for gadgets that only ship a Windows vendor app, such as a case LCD, an RGB controller, a mouse or a "smart" lamp. No hardware is needed to try it.

From captures of the NZXT Kraken X (1e71:170e) fan command, it recovers 02 4d <channel> 00 <duty> byte for byte, as liquidctl's kraken2.py sends it, and the generated driver emits identical packets for duty values it never saw. The same holds for the SteelSeries Rival 100 DPI, polling and RGB tables from rivalcfg. Those checks run in CI; details are in validation .

On Arch Linux, use pipx install usb-rea instead; the FAQ has the packages for capture.

mode 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x30 | lookup 1→0x11, 2→0x22, 3→0x47 | 0x00 | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

fan 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x10 | u16be round(value * 1 + 0) | 0x00 | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color 100% 0x5a | counter (+1 per message) | 0x20 | RGB bytes | u16le crc16_modbus(bytes[0:6])

color only sent while mode 3: the driver sets it first

It writes a synthetic capture of a fan controller, recovers the protocol and the replies, and writes report.md (every claim linked to Wireshark frame numbers) plus a working pyusb driver. --device lamp is a simpler 8-bit device; --device lcd is a pump cap screen; --device dial shows 32-bit values and packed bitfields.

On a real device, label each click in the vendor app, then infer:

usb-rea mark -m lamp.pcapng.actions.json " brightness 0% " # then click it; 3+ values per setting

usb-rea scaffold lamp.pcapng -o lamp_driver.py

Captured on Windows with USBPcap and no markers? List the actions in order and usb-rea splits the traffic at the pauses. The full CLI, including markers, replies, handshakes, image streams and HID, is in usage .

Before you capture, usb-rea lookup 1e71:170e (or the ID 1e71:170e form from lsusb ) checks a VID:PID against devices whose protocol an open-source project already implements. The offline table is in known devices .

Status: alpha (v0.7.14, on PyPI ). It is validated on synthetic devices, on protocols documented by liquidctl and rivalcfg, on public Wireshark captures, and on a real AIO cooler LCD capture a user shared. Linear fits must survive leave-one-out cross-checks; otherwise usb-rea falls back to a lookup table and says so. A matching USB ID alone does not prove your unit speaks the same protocol.

How this differs from Wireshark is in the FAQ .

Reverse engineering for interoperability is permitted (EU Directive 2009/24/EC Art. 6, US DMCA §1201(f)). usb-rea only analyzes traffic of devices you own and never redistributes vendor code.

Have a Windows-only device? Open a device request with a capture and I will run it and publish the result.

Usage: capture, markers, inference and the generated driver

MCP Registry name: io.github.emirmrkaljevic/usb-rea

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: CyberLeek has released the GTA 6 executable file for Xbox version 1.0.2.1 three hours ahead of schedule.
items.content:
On November 23, 2026, an anonymous hacker using the pseudonym CyberLeek published the main executable file (EXE) for the Xbox console version of Grand Theft Auto VI. The release of build 1.0.2.1 occurred three hours before the scheduled end of the timer. Earlier, on November 19, the same source posted a decrypted archive containing the game's main resources, approximately 209 GB in size, which was missing the executable module. The archive containing the new file was posted on several file-sharing services, and to confirm its authenticity, the author provided SHA-256 checksums for the ZIP archive itself and the executable file contained within. CyberLeek specifically emphasized that regular users should not attempt to run this file on Windows, as it will not work directly and is intended solely for developers of open source emulation and static recompilation projects.

The release of the executable file removes the main limitation for enthusiasts who have been studying the leaked November build of GTA 6 for the Xbox Series X and S consoles for several days. Since Microsoft consoles use the x86-64 architecture based on AMD Zen 2 processors and the GDK development environment, which is close to Windows, several independent projects on GitHub, including Leonida, Xbox2Windows and AnyXboxX have already begun adapting the code. Until now, developers could only analyze auxiliary libraries and translate RDNA 2 shaders into SPIR-V formats for Vulkan or DXIL for DirectX 12, but the lack of the main EXE file prevented the acquisition of root signature tables for mesh shaders and the launch of the game. CyberLeek previously stated that after receiving the final component, the community would be able to run the game via emulation on PC within a week, with a frame rate exceeding the console's 30 FPS.

The file's publication was accompanied by a statement from the author, in which he declared all his releases free and called for support through donations in Bitcoin and Monero cryptocurrencies, as well as through trading the CYBERLEEK token. Initially, the early release of the executable was tied to reaching a token market cap of $15 million; this threshold was later lowered to $6 million, but ultimately, the release took place on schedule, slightly ahead of schedule. Rockstar Games has not yet commented on the authenticity of the distributed files, although the studio has previously made it clear that it intends to strictly suppress any attempts to create unofficial PC ports. Security experts also warn that downloading unofficial builds carries a risk of malware infection due to the large number of fake websites that replicate the hacker's original resource.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

items.title: Landlord’s AI Makes Rent Deal With Woman, Actual Landlord Breaks Deal and Evicts Her: "It's ridiculous."
items.content:
It turns out that double-dealing is fine if an AI chatbot is doing it on your behalf.

A North Carolina woman says her landlord evicted her despite receiving an email from the leasing office saying she’d have an extension to pay her $4,000 in overdue rent. That official communication, it turned out, was written by the landlord’s AI assistant, who claims that the AI did so without their knowledge, according to WRAL News .

Now the tenant, Laura Mack, has gone to court to try reverse the eviction. She says she feels deceived because there was no obvious indication at the time that she was communicating with an AI. The sympathetic emails sounded, to her, human. Unfortunately, it was the humans here who would ultimately prove heartless.

“I’m baffled,” Mack said. “I need a place to stay.”

The situation raises a hairy question in an era when many industries are rushing to automate communications : if the landlord is choosing to let AI represent them, can they go back on their, or their AI’s, word?

The emails from Colony Townhome Apartments, viewed by WRAL , showed the AI asking what date would work best for her to pay before approving her request: “Paying on November 30, the last day of the month, works,” it said.

Then, days later, she received an abrupt eviction notice. When Mack confronted the leasing office, the leasing agent allegedly said that it was the AI agent, Olivia, that had been emailing her and mistakenly granted her an extension.

According to WRAL , the complex informed residents back in December 2025 that the new AI agent could handle their rent and maintenance questions. Normally, Olivia’s messages are supposed to be marked as coming from an AI, but the ones that Mack received showed no disclosure. In fact, the AI sounded awfully compassionate and knowledgeable about her situation.

“I also know you’re dealing with the hole in the downstairs bathroom ceiling,” the AI wrote at one point, per WRAL . “I’m sorry you’re dealing with that.”

The emails were signed, “Best regards, Colony Townhome Apartments.”

“I thought it was someone from the office because all my information was in there and it mentioned my bathroom,” Mack told the news station.

The incident has infuriated local lawmakers.

“It’s ridiculous,” state senator Jim Burgin said in an interview with WRAL Friday. “I think notification is one thing, and I think liability is another.”

“Before someone evicted that lady, they should have reviewed their documents,” he added.

Burgin has proposed a “Bot Bill” that would require users be informed whenever they’re communicating with an AI, but in the past three years that he’s tried introducing it, it hasn’t advanced in the legislature, per WRAL .

Mack is now living out of a hotel until she finds a permanent place to stay — or wins her battle in court.

“If you told me till the 30th, I’ll get out by the 30th,” Mack said. “But give me that. You at least honor that. You have to have somewhere where you’re taking responsibility.”

items.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
items.content:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel

module ( xnu.ko ) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS

processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its

memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module ( fki.ko ).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the

desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 ( sw_vers , the Darwin kernel, launchd,

WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,

Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).

Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.

The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).

Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the

hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on ( GPU=auto ).

macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)

────────────────────────────────────────────────── ────────────────────────────────────────────

XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │

↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)

xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)

↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)

fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)

Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)

CPUs : each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host

(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of

Memory : XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux

share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).

Devices : kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a

keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.

GPU : Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux

host's GPU through the DRM bridge ( kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using

Mesa's Venus driver; without a GPU it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.

Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs:

macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).

Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes,

Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.

Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each

The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU ( Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max) ) and is enabled by default

( GPU=auto ) when a Linux render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering ( GPU=off ) otherwise.

What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md . Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into

the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

An arm64 Linux host with PAC (Apple Silicon M1 or later in a VM: krunkit for GPU access, or tart), 4K pages, 16 GB of

RAM (8 GB of it reserved for the hosted kernel).

items.title: UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity
items.summary: compsci, science
items.content:
UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the  School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden said.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek said.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.)

Professor Matthew Davis said the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis said.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances .

For those who don't know me, let me introduce myself. I'm the independent developer behind FSNotes , an open-source note-taking app for macOS and iOS.

I've been developing FSNotes for 9 years. And what happened a few weeks ago came as a complete shock.

Apple removed my app from every European App Store. Without a clear explanation or any way to resolve the issue promptly.

It all started when I didn't receive my October sales payout. This had happened before, but I was usually able to resolve it by contacting Apple Support. Not this time.

Since November 5, I haven't received a single response. Not one.

I've gone through everything I could find in App Store Connect, completed the necessary compliance information under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA), and submitted official documents from Ukraine's government business registry.

I'm a legally registered sole proprietor in Ukraine. I run my business officially and pay my taxes. But apparently, that's not enough. Or perhaps nobody is even reviewing my documents.

And you know what's the most frustrating part?

While Apple remains silent, everything I've spent nine years building is being destroyed.

My app is losing its positions in App Store rankings and search results. The visibility, reputation, and discoverability I've worked so hard to build over the years are disappearing right before my eyes.

Even if Apple restores my app tomorrow, who's going to give me those rankings back? Who will compensate me for the lost time, users, and revenue?

I'm not asking for special treatment. I'm not asking Apple to bend the rules for me. I simply want someone to review my documents, explain the restrictions, and give me a chance to resolve the issue.

It's especially painful to see how difficult it has become for a Ukrainian developer to keep working. Sometimes it feels like Ukraine is the country under sanctions, not Russia.

FSNotes is still available for free on GitHub. I'll continue providing access to the source code and free builds. But the reality is that without revenue, it will be extremely difficult for an independent project like this to survive.

I'm asking you to support this open letter to Apple with a like or a repost. I'm not asking for donations or special privileges. I just want to bring this situation to the attention of the App Store team.

You cannot simply remove an app with a nine-year history from sale, ignore a developer's support requests for weeks, and provide no explanation of what's happening.

This kind of treatment is killing indie development.

items.title: Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree
items.summary: clojure
items.content:
Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree

Until recently, sorted-map and sorted-set in Jolt were a straight port of Clojure's PersistentTreeMap , which is backed by a persistent red-black tree. Using a red-black tree has worked well for Clojure, and it provides a solid foundation for backing these data structures. However, red-black trees have a downside, which is that every entry gets its own small node, meaning that every step of a lookup follows a pointer to a different place in memory.

So, naturally I got curious to see if a different data structure could be used for the same job which might have a lower overhead. Turns out that a red-black tree can indeed be swapped out for a B+tree here. I updated Jolt's sorted collections along with the java.util.TreeMap and TreeSet shims to use a persistent B+tree, which dropped peak memory by 40% while making most operations faster at every size, as we'll see later in the benchmarks.

Each red-black node in Jolt was a five-slot Scheme vector holding a color along with the key, the value, and its two children. And all that translates into 48 bytes of metadata per entry on top of the key and value themselves. A map with 4 million entries needs a tree around 22 levels deep, so, a lookup can end up visiting about 22 nodes scattered across the heap. And once the tree outgrows the CPU cache, each of these visits is likely to be a cache miss as well.

As you might've guessed, writes also have a similar problem. Since a persistent tree can't modify a node in place, an assoc has to copy every node on the path from the root to the change, which results in 22 small allocations followed by rebalancing at that size.

The key advantage of using a B+tree is that it keeps data in leaves of up to 16 entries and branches through inner nodes of up to 32 children with each node being a single Scheme vector. In this layout, a leaf is written as #(#t k0 v0 k1 v1 ...) with keys and values sitting side by side in one contiguous block. An inner node also stores the largest key below it right next to each child.

Now, the same tree of 4 million entries becomes just 5 levels deep instead of 22. On top of that, a lookup within each node has to only search through adjacent slots that are already in cache. Writes still have to copy the path from the root, but that's now a quarter of the work with each one being copied as a block.

Unsurprisingly, memory use improved significantly, since a full leaf holds 16 entries in 34 machine words, needing only 17 bytes per entry against the red-black tree's 48. Nodes are also allowed to drop to half before they merge, so 34 bytes per entry ends up being the worst case here. It would be ideal to keep the common case near full as much as possible, and a trick that can be used here is to start a fresh node when append goes past either end of the tree rather than splitting a full node into two half-empty ones. A common case for this would be building from ascending keys, which ends up packing every node using this approach. Similarly, deletes end up borrowing entries from a neighbour or merging with it to keep the tree balanced without needing rotations.

Of course, nothing in life is free, and B+trees do have a weakness of their own. While they're much faster for large collections, building small ones of tens to hundreds of entries one insert at a time ended up being around 15% slower than the red-black tree. The reason goes back to the respective structure of each data structure. Once a map has 17 entries, that requires a root with two leaves, and every insert needs to copy the whole path. So, at smaller sizes the B+tree has to move more bytes per insert than the red-black tree, which is the trade-off.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Trump tells CNBC ‘I convinced’ Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang
items.content:
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday morning that he spoke directly to Nvidia 's board and urged them to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang .

"I spoke to them, let me put it that way," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview shortly after Nvidia's shock announcement that Huang was returning to lead the tech giant.

"And I convinced them," the president said. "I made the deal."

Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang came less than two weeks after he resigned. Huang had stepped down after admitting he cheated on his wife and amid claims his affairs included one with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.

Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, and her role as an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed raised concerns that she was facilitating the diversion of Nvidia's most advanced semiconductor chip to China.

Trump said Nvidia's board "did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said.

"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot," the president said.

Trump said that after he spoke with Nvidia's board, "when the deal was finished," he called Huang.

"I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said.

"I didn't talk about other things because he understands that. He understands it better than we do," the president said. "He knows what to do and what not to do. But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close."

Trump also told CNBC that Huang "did nothing wrong."

"I think the [Nvidia] board acted really responsibly" in deciding to bring Huang back.

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president said.

"I'm very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly," the president said.

Asked whether the broad stock market selloff last week after Huang's resignation from Nvidia factored into his decision to push for the CEO's reinstatement, Trump said, "Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term."

"The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about," Trump said.

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

Get the latest cybersecurity news, critical vulnerabilities, threat intelligence, tutorials, and exclusive giveaways delivered straight to your inbox. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.
